name: Load Balancing
intent: Spread incoming requests across several servers so none is overloaded, and so the service keeps working when one server dies.
scenario: An online shop runs on three servers. Customers all use one address, and something has to decide which server answers each request.
problem: A single server has a ceiling on CPU, memory and connections. Traffic above it queues or fails, and if that one machine dies the whole site is down. Adding servers only helps if requests are actually shared between them, and clients should not need to know how many servers exist or which are healthy.

howItWorks.title: Clients talk to one address
howItWorks.text: DNS or a virtual IP points at the load balancer, not at any server. Clients never learn the servers' addresses, so servers can be added or removed freely.

howItWorks.title: The balancer picks a server
howItWorks.text: An algorithm chooses the target. Round robin takes turns. Least connections picks the server with the fewest requests in flight. Weighted variants send more to bigger machines. Hashing sends the same client to the same server.

howItWorks.title: Health checks keep dead servers out
howItWorks.text: The balancer probes each server regularly. A server that fails is taken out of rotation, and put back when it recovers, so users do not hit a dead machine.

howItWorks.title: The request is forwarded and the answer returned
howItWorks.text: A layer 4 balancer routes raw TCP connections. A layer 7 balancer understands HTTP and can route by path, header or cookie, and terminate TLS in one place.

howItWorks.title: The balancer must not be a single point of failure
howItWorks.text: Run at least two balancers (active-passive with a floating IP, or active-active), or use a managed service. Otherwise you have only moved the single point of failure.

pros: Spreads load, so capacity grows by adding servers (horizontal scaling)
Survives server failures: traffic skips unhealthy machines
Enables zero-downtime deploys by draining one server at a time
One place for TLS, routing rules and rate limits
cons: An extra network hop, and the balancer itself needs redundancy
Stateful apps need sticky sessions or a shared session store
Simple algorithms ignore how expensive each request is
Health checks add configuration and can cause flapping if tuned badly
whenToUse: More than one server runs the same service
You want to deploy or patch without downtime
Traffic is bursty and you need headroom and failover
You want to route by URL path to different backends (layer 7)
whenNotToUse: One small server comfortably handles the traffic and downtime is acceptable
Each client must reach one specific node that owns its data: use sharding with consistent hashing instead
Internal tools with a handful of users
pitfalls: Sticky sessions pin users to one server and quietly defeat the balancing
A health check that only tests an open port will keep sending traffic to a broken app
Round robin treats a heavy request and a light one as equal, so one server can still pile up
A recovered server that instantly receives full traffic can fall over again
Cached DNS answers can keep clients on a removed balancer
